As the founder of Kid One, an organization that has transported thousands of young patients to their appointments, Jackson understands the scope of the problem firsthand. "We discovered that more than 80,000 children across Alabama were living in households without a vehicle," he explains. "And in rural regions, there's simply no public transportation available—no cabs, no buses, no trains. Across our nation, millions of children face this same barrier to healthcare every single day."

This conviction ran so deep that Jackson walked away from his firefighting career in Alabama back in 1997, relocated to stay with friends, and tapped into his retirement savings to launch Kid One Transport, a charitable organization dedicated to driving underprivileged children to medical visits throughout the state. Over the course of 11 years, the organization's vans have completed rides for upward of 16,000 children heading to and from their scheduled healthcare appointments across Alabama.

Leaving the fire department to run a charity was never part of Jackson's plan—becoming a firefighter had been his childhood dream come true. "What kid doesn't dream of being a firefighter?" he asks with a chuckle. Everything shifted, however, following a devastating call his crew responded to in March 1992. A 2-year-old had accidentally strangled himself while reaching for a toy inside the family vehicle, and Jackson's team was called to assist. "We did everything possible to try to save that child's life," he recalls. Despite their efforts, the toddler didn't survive.

"That one really got to me," Jackson admits. "I'd seen tragic situations before, but something about this was different." Following a counselor's recommendation, he turned to volunteer work as a way to cope with his grief. A friend pointed him toward the small town of Sayre, Alabama, and what he encountered there—just a 25-minute drive from his own house—left him shaken. "Entering that community felt like stepping into an entirely different world. So many of the homes were in terrible condition—there's really no other way to describe it," he says. The stark contrast to his own comfortable life filled him with immediate guilt.

"One visit was all it took," he remembers. "I knew right then I wanted to work alongside these people and do everything within my power to ease their burdens." Once local social workers explained that neighborhood kids had no means of getting to chemotherapy sessions, physical therapy, or basic checkups, Jackson began personally driving them himself. What started as a solo effort eventually expanded into a fleet of 13 vans serving 30 counties.

Although Jackson has since stepped back from the organization's daily operations, he considers connecting with families and witnessing medical breakthroughs the most rewarding part of his journey—children who learned to talk, others who took their first steps, and some who overcame serious illnesses even when doctors offered little hope.

"I witnessed so much transformation—children and parents determined to defy the odds stacked against them," he reflects, crediting reliable transportation as the key factor. "We fill that missing piece that keeps so many families from accessing world-class medical care... Knowing they overcame everything simply because we provided a ride," he adds, "makes founding Kid One Transport absolutely worthwhile."

# Kid One Transport: Driving Change for Alabama's Children

In 1997, Russell Jackson founded Kid One Transport, a nonprofit organization dedicated to providing free medical transportation for children in need throughout Alabama. What began as a response to a personal tragedy has since grown into a vital lifeline for thousands of families who might otherwise have no way to access essential healthcare services for their children.

The need for such a service in Alabama is staggering. More than 80,000 children in the state live in households without access to a car, a reality that becomes even more challenging in rural areas where public transportation options like buses, trains, or taxis are often nonexistent. For these families, a medical appointment—whether routine or urgent—can become an insurmountable obstacle simply due to a lack of reliable transportation. Kid One Transport was created to bridge this gap, ensuring that a child's access to healthcare is not determined by their family's financial situation or geographic location.

Over its eleven years of operation, Kid One's fleet of vans has made an extraordinary impact, transporting more than 16,000 children to critical medical appointments across the state. These rides have connected countless families with doctors, specialists, and treatments they would have otherwise been unable to reach, transforming the organization from a small startup into an indispensable community resource.

The origins of Kid One Transport are deeply rooted in personal loss and a search for meaning. Jackson, who once worked as a firefighter, made the difficult decision to leave his career behind, using his own retirement savings to launch the nonprofit. His path to this life-changing decision began in 1992, during a devastating emergency call that would forever alter his perspective. The call involved the death of a 2-year-old child, an experience so traumatic that it left Jackson grappling with grief and searching for a way to cope with what he had witnessed.

In the aftermath of this tragedy, a counselor suggested that Jackson consider volunteer work as a way to process his emotions and find purpose again. This advice led him to a rural community in Alabama, where he came face-to-face with a different kind of crisis: families desperately in need of transportation to access basic medical care for their children. Witnessing this urgent, unmet need firsthand ignited something in Jackson—a determination to create a solution. That determination ultimately became Kid One Transport, an organization born out of heartbreak but sustained by hope, compassion, and an unwavering commitment to ensuring that no child in Alabama is denied medical care simply because their family lacks a way to get there.

# From Tragedy to Transportation: The Story of Kid One Transport

## A Firefighter's Turning Point

Russell Jackson spent years as a firefighter in Alabama, responding to emergencies and witnessing firsthand the fragility of life in his community. But one call would change the trajectory of his career and, ultimately, the lives of thousands of children across the state. Jackson responded to the death of a child—a death that, he came to believe, might have been prevented if the family had simply had access to reliable transportation to get proper medical care in time. The tragedy haunted him, and rather than letting it fade into memory, he decided to act.

## Identifying a Hidden Crisis

As Jackson looked deeper into the issue, he uncovered a problem that was far more widespread than he had initially realized. Across rural Alabama, tens of thousands of children from low-income families were missing critical medical appointments—not because their families didn't care or doctors weren't available, but because there was no way to get them there. Many rural areas lacked public transportation systems entirely, and families without reliable vehicles found themselves with no options when a child needed to see a doctor, attend a follow-up appointment, or receive ongoing treatment for chronic conditions.

This transportation gap created a silent barrier to healthcare—one that didn't show up in insurance statistics or hospital records, but that had very real consequences for children's health and wellbeing. Missed appointments meant delayed diagnoses, untreated conditions, and preventable complications, disproportionately affecting families already struggling with poverty in underserved rural communities.

## Building a Solution: Kid One Transport

In 1997, Jackson took action by founding Kid One Transport, a nonprofit organization dedicated to solving this specific problem. The mission was straightforward but powerful: provide safe, reliable transportation to ensure that no child would miss essential medical care simply because their family lacked a way to get there.

Starting a nonprofit from the ground up presented significant challenges—securing funding, acquiring vehicles, hiring and training drivers, and building the infrastructure needed to coordinate rides for children across rural areas. But Jackson's firsthand understanding of the problem, born from that painful firefighting experience, gave him the motivation to push through the obstacles.

## Eleven Years of Impact

Over the following eleven years, Kid One Transport grew into a vital community resource. The organization built up a fleet of vans specifically dedicated to transporting children to their medical appointments—whether routine checkups, specialist visits, therapy sessions, or treatments for chronic illnesses. Drivers and coordinators worked to ensure that transportation barriers no longer stood between rural children and the healthcare they needed.

The results speak for themselves: by 2008, Kid One Transport had successfully transported more than 16,000 children to their medical appointments. Each of those trips represented a child who received care they might otherwise have missed—a diagnosis caught early, a treatment continued without interruption, a health crisis averted.

## A Model for Addressing Healthcare Access

Jackson's organization stands as a powerful example of how identifying and addressing a specific, often-overlooked barrier can create substantial change. Transportation is frequently an invisible obstacle in discussions about healthcare access, overshadowed by conversations about insurance coverage, provider availability, and treatment costs. Yet for families in rural areas without reliable vehicles or public transit options, the inability to physically get to an appointment can be just as significant a barrier as any of these more commonly discussed issues.

Kid One Transport's success demonstrates that sometimes the most effective solutions to complex problems are remarkably direct: if families can't get to healthcare, bring reliable transportation to them. What began as one man's response to personal tragedy evolved into a sustainable, impactful nonprofit model that continues to serve as a lifeline for underserved children and families, ensuring that geography and poverty don't become insurmountable obstacles to essential medical care.

Birmingham, Alabama, stands as one of the most significant cities in American history, particularly regarding the civil rights movement. Founded in 1871, the city grew rapidly due to its iron and steel industry, earning it the nickname "The Magic City" and later "The Pittsburgh of the South."

However, Birmingham's most profound legacy lies in the 1960s, when it became a central battleground for civil rights. The city gained national and international attention through extensive **CNN** coverage and other media outlets that documented the brutal realities of segregation. Images of peaceful protesters, including children, being attacked with fire hoses and police dogs shocked the nation's conscience and helped galvanize support for civil rights legislation.

Key events that defined this era include:

- The 1963 Birmingham campaign led by Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.
- The tragic bombing of the 16th Street Baptist Church, which killed four young girls
- King's famous "Letter from Birmingham Jail"

Media coverage, which would later be extensively analyzed and referenced by networks like CNN in retrospective documentaries, played a crucial role in exposing these injustices to a national audience. This coverage helped build momentum for the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

Today, Birmingham has transformed significantly. The city honors its complex history through institutions like the Birmingham Civil Rights Institute and Kelly Ingram Park, which serve as memorials to those who fought for justice. Modern Birmingham has diversified its economy, focusing on healthcare, banking, and technology sectors, moving beyond its industrial roots.

CNN and other major news organizations continue to report on Birmingham periodically, whether covering historical anniversaries, economic developments, or the city's ongoing efforts at reconciliation and growth. Birmingham's story represents both a painful chapter in American history and a testament to resilience and change, making it a city that continues to reflect broader national conversations about race, justice, and progress.

# From Fire Trucks to Front Seats: How One Firefighter Is Driving Change for Rural Families

*The volunteer service he started with a borrowed van now brings hope to hundreds of families who once faced impossible choices between medical care and financial ruin*

---

**MOUNTAIN VIEW, [STATE]** — Captain Danny Reeves has spent 15 years racing toward emergencies. But it wasn't a fire that changed the trajectory of his life — it was a phone call from a mother who couldn't figure out how to get her son to a cancer treatment 120 miles away.

"She was crying, asking me if I knew anyone who could help," Reeves recalls. "Her car had broken down, her husband couldn't take more time off work, and the nearest oncology center was two and a half hours away. That's when it hit me — we run toward burning buildings, but who's showing up for families just trying to survive the day-to-day?"

That phone call in 2019 became the spark for Wheels of Hope, a nonprofit Reeves founded that provides free transportation for children in rural communities to essential medical appointments — dialysis, chemotherapy, specialist visits, and follow-up care that many urban families take for granted.

## A Gap Nobody Was Talking About

For families in rural America, distance isn't just an inconvenience — it can be a matter of life and death. According to health policy researchers, rural residents travel significantly farther for specialty care, and lack of transportation is consistently cited as one of the top reasons pediatric patients miss critical appointments.

"People don't think about it until they're living it," Reeves says. "You've got a kid who needs weekly treatment, but you live an hour from the nearest gas station, let alone a children's hospital. Insurance doesn't cover a ride. Public transit doesn't exist. So what happens? Sometimes the treatment just... stops."

Reeves saw this firsthand, responding to emergency calls in communities where the nearest hospital was sometimes an hour or more away by ambulance. He began noticing a pattern: families who weren't calling 911, but who were quietly falling through the cracks of a system not built for people who live far from cities.

## From One Van to a Fleet

Reeves started small — using his own truck and gas money to drive a handful of children to appointments on his days off from the fire station. Word spread quickly through church groups, school nurses, and rural clinics desperate for a solution.

Today, Wheels of Hope operates a fleet of six vehicles, staffed by a mix of paid drivers and background-checked volunteers, many of them fellow firefighters and first responders who understand the value of showing up when it matters most.

"These guys already have hearts wired for service," Reeves says of his volunteer drivers. "It wasn't hard to get firefighters on board. We're used to answering the call — this is just a different kind of call."

The nonprofit has provided more than 3,000 rides since its founding, connecting children with treatments for conditions ranging from leukemia to congenital heart defects to severe asthma requiring specialist care unavailable locally.

## More Than Just a Ride

For families like the Talbots, whose 8-year-old daughter Ellie has undergone years of treatment for a rare kidney disorder, Wheels of Hope has become a lifeline that goes beyond transportation.

"Danny doesn't just drop her off," says Sarah Talbot, Ellie's mother. "He knows her favorite songs. He remembers her doctor's name. He asks about her stuffed animals. For an hour and a half each way, my daughter isn't a patient — she's just a kid talking to her buddy Danny."

Reeves insists these relationships are the point. "Anybody can drive a car. What we're really doing is making sure these kids know somebody cares whether they show up or not."

The organization has expanded services to include care packages for long hospital stays, coordination with local clinics for scheduling, and even overnight stays for families who need to travel long distances for early morning appointments.

## Balancing Two Callings

Reeves still works full shifts at the fire station, squeezing in nonprofit responsibilities during off-hours and rest days. His wife, Melissa, jokes that their family calendar looks like "air traffic control."

"There were times I wondered if he was stretching himself too thin," Melissa admits. "But then you see a mom send a text saying her son made it to his transplant evaluation because of us, and you understand why he can't stop."

Reeves is quick to deflect credit, pointing instead to the growing network of volunteers, local business sponsors who donate fuel and vehicle maintenance, and community fundraisers that keep the organization running.

"This was never about me," he says. "It's about making sure a kid in a farmhouse at the end of a gravel road has the same shot at getting better as a kid who lives five minutes from the hospital."

## What's Next

Reeves hopes to expand Wheels of Hope into three additional counties within the next two years, and he's begun mentoring other first responders interested in launching similar programs in their own underserved communities.

"If just one firefighter in another rural town reads this and thinks, 'I could do that too' — that's the whole mission working," Reeves says. "We can't wait for someone else to fix it. Sometimes you have to be the ride you wish existed."

For now, Reeves continues his dual life — badge on one day, steering wheel the next — proving that heroism doesn't always look like flashing lights and sirens. Sometimes, it looks like an open car door and a familiar voice saying, *"Ready to go, kiddo?"*

---

# The Wheels of Hope

When Marcus Webb was working as a logistics manager for a shipping company in Birmingham, Alabama, he thought he understood transportation problems. Then he met an eight-year-old girl named Destiny.

Destiny had leukemia. Her treatment required trips to Children's of Alabama—three times a week, sometimes more—but her family lived in rural Wilcox County, nearly two hours away. Her mother worked two jobs and didn't own a reliable car. More than once, Destiny missed critical chemotherapy appointments simply because there was no way to get there.

Marcus learned about Destiny's situation through his church's prayer list. What started as arranging a single ride turned into something that would consume the next chapter of his life.

"I kept thinking about how many other Destinys there must be," Marcus recalls. "Kids who weren't missing treatment because the medicine wasn't there, or because doctors weren't available—but because of miles. Because of gas money. Because of broken-down cars sitting in driveways."

In 2019, Marcus did the math on his own finances, talked it over with his wife, and quit his job. He sold his boat, cashed in part of his 401k, and bought a used minivan. He named his nonprofit **Miles for Miracles**.

At first, it was just Marcus driving. He'd wake up at 4 a.m. to pick up a child in Selma for a 9 a.m. appointment in Birmingham, then turn around and do it again in reverse that evening. He slept in his van more nights than he can count.

Word spread. A retired nurse volunteered to ride along and monitor kids who needed oxygen during transport. A local mechanic began fixing up donated vehicles for free. Churches organized gas card drives. Within two years, Miles for Miracles had a fleet of twelve vehicles and forty trained volunteer drivers, covering fourteen counties across Alabama's Black Belt—one of the most medically underserved regions in the country.

Today, the organization has provided more than 15,000 rides to children battling cancer, congenital heart defects, sickle cell disease, and other serious illnesses. Marcus's team doesn't just drive—they've become family to the children they serve. Drivers know the kids' favorite songs, their allergies, which ones need a stuffed animal within reach during a rough patch.

Destiny, now fourteen, is in remission. She still remembers the first time Marcus picked her up.

"He had snacks in the car and let me choose the radio station," she says, laughing. "I didn't feel like a sick kid. I just felt like a kid going somewhere."

Marcus doesn't take credit easily. "I didn't cure anybody," he says. "I just made sure they had the chance to get the medicine that could."

But for families across rural Alabama, that chance has meant everything.

---

*Miles for Miracles is currently raising funds to expand into three additional counties and purchase two wheelchair-accessible vans. To nominate Marcus Webb or learn more about supporting his mission, visit CNNHeroes.com.*

# When Tragedy Became a Mission: How One Firefighter's Worst Call Sparked a Lifeline for Rural Kids

The call came in on a Tuesday afternoon, one of thousands that volunteer firefighter Mark Ostrander had responded to in his fifteen years with the department. But this one would change everything.

A young girl, no more than seven, was in respiratory distress. Her family lived nearly 40 miles from the nearest hospital equipped to handle her condition, down a stretch of unpaved county road that turned to mud after rain. By the time Ostrander's crew arrived and stabilized her enough for transport, critical time had been lost. She didn't survive the ambulance ride.

"I remember standing in that driveway afterward," Ostrander recalls, "and thinking, this shouldn't happen in this country. Not because we don't have the medicine. Because we don't have the road."

That moment—equal parts grief and fury—became the seed for what is now Roads to Care, a nonprofit organization Ostrander founded eighteen months later. The organization's mission is deceptively simple: eliminate the transportation barriers that keep rural children from reaching medical treatment in time.

## The Hidden Crisis

Rural healthcare access has long been a documented problem in America, but Ostrander's organization zeroes in on a specific, often-overlooked piece of it: the gap between diagnosis and treatment when families lack reliable transportation.

"Everyone talks about hospital closures and doctor shortages," says Dr. Elena Vasquez, a pediatric specialist who now consults for Roads to Care. "But nobody talks about the mother with three other kids and no car who can't get her son to chemotherapy sixty miles away. Nobody talks about the family that misses a specialist appointment because their truck broke down and there's no bus, no rideshare, nothing."

Roads to Care has since coordinated over 3,000 rides for children needing everything from routine checkups to ongoing cancer treatment. The organization operates a fleet of volunteer drivers, partners with local fire departments for emergency situations, and has begun lobbying state legislators for rural transportation infrastructure funding.

## From Grief to Action

Ostrander, now 43, still serves as a volunteer firefighter but has scaled back his hours to run the nonprofit full-time. He's quick to deflect credit, insisting the organization is powered by "an army of people who just needed somewhere to put their frustration."

That frustration has translated into a network spanning four counties, with dozens of volunteer drivers who log thousands of miles monthly. Local businesses have donated vehicles. A regional hospital system now partners with Roads to Care to identify families at risk of missing appointments.

The girl who died that Tuesday afternoon—her family asked that her name not be used publicly—has nonetheless become part of the organization's quiet mythology. Volunteers know her story. It's why they show up.

"I can't tell you her name," Ostrander says, "but I can tell you she's the reason a kid in Millbrook made it to his dialysis appointment yesterday. That's not nothing. That has to count for something."

## Looking Forward

Roads to Care recently received a grant that will allow it to expand into two additional counties, and Ostrander has begun consulting with organizers in other states hoping to replicate the model.

He's careful, though, not to frame the work as redemption arc or triumph over tragedy. Some days, he says, are still hard. He still remembers every detail of that call.

"This isn't a story about me feeling better," he says. "It's about making sure the next family doesn't have to feel what that family felt. If I can do that, even once more, then something good came out of the worst day of my career."

For the families in rural communities who now have a ride to the doctor, a way to reach the hospital, a lifeline that didn't exist eighteen months ago, that's more than enough.

# When Distance Becomes a Matter of Life and Death: How One Woman's Mission Is Getting Alabama's Sickest Kids to Care

*Reported in the style of CNN.com*

BIRMINGHAM, Alabama — For families in Alabama's rural counties, a child's cancer diagnosis or premature birth doesn't just bring fear and uncertainty. It brings a logistical nightmare that can mean the difference between a life saved and a life lost: How do you get a critically ill child 100 miles down a two-lane highway to the only specialist who can help, especially when you don't have a reliable car, gas money, or the ability to miss another day of minimum-wage work?

For more than three decades, one Birmingham-based nonprofit has been quietly solving that problem, one ride at a time.

Kid One Transport System has driven more than a million miles and helped tens of thousands of Alabama children reach medical appointments they otherwise might have missed entirely — dialysis treatments, chemotherapy, specialist visits, early intervention therapy — the unglamorous but essential infrastructure of pediatric health care in a state where rural hospital closures and physician shortages have left entire counties without basic services.

## A Mother's Desperation Becomes a Movement

The organization's origin story is, like so many nonprofits born from necessity, deeply personal.

Kid One was founded in 1989 by Elizabeth "Sister" Sherrod, a Birmingham nurse who had spent years watching families in her care miss critical appointments — not from negligence, but from impossibility. Parents without cars. Single mothers who couldn't afford to lose a shift. Grandparents raising sick grandchildren with no way to get them 90 minutes to Children's of Alabama, the state's premier pediatric hospital.

Sherrod had seen the consequences up close: a child's asthma spiraling into an ICU admission because a follow-up visit got missed; a preemie's developmental delays compounding because early therapy sessions kept falling through. The medicine existed. The doctors existed. What didn't exist was a way to connect vulnerable families to either.

So she started driving kids herself.

What began as one nurse and her own car has grown into a fleet of specially equipped vehicles — including vans outfitted for wheelchairs and medical equipment — serving dozens of counties across Alabama, a state where nearly one in five children lives in poverty and where the gap between urban medical resources and rural access remains stark.

## The Ripple Effects of a Ride

The impact of Kid One's work extends far beyond the individual trips logged. Health researchers have long identified transportation as one of the most under-recognized "social determinants of health" — the non-medical factors that shape whether people can actually access the care available to them. A missed appointment isn't just an inconvenience; for a child with cancer or kidney failure, it can mean a treatment plan derailed, an infection untreated, a condition allowed to worsen.

For rural Alabama families, many of them working poor, the organization has become a kind of invisible scaffolding holding together fragile care plans. Parents who spoke of the service described drivers who became familiar, trusted faces — sometimes the only adults besides medical staff who saw their child regularly through months of grueling treatment.

The organization has also adapted over the years, expanding services to include rides for prenatal care, mental health appointments, and early intervention services for children with developmental disabilities — recognizing that health outcomes are shaped as much by consistent access as by any single medical breakthrough.

## A Legacy Rooted in Persistence

Sherrod, who led the organization for years after its founding, built Kid One not as a stopgap but as permanent infrastructure — proof that community-based, grassroots solutions can fill gaps that policy and hospital systems often leave open. Her work reflected a broader truth increasingly recognized in public health circles: that in America's most under-resourced regions, the barrier to care is often not medicine itself, but the miles between a family and the nearest place to receive it.

Today, Kid One Transport continues to operate on a combination of grants, donations, and community support, a reminder that in a state still grappling with rural hospital closures and stubborn health disparities, sometimes the most vital medical intervention isn't a new drug or a new procedure — it's simply a ride.
